entry.title: Preventing Software Crashes from Culture-Sensitive String Casing Using Invariant Culture Settings
entry.summary:
The Anatomy of a Crash
Software stability relies on the silent assumption that basic data types behave identically everywhere on Earth. But when a software application executes a default string transformation on a device configured for a regional locale like Turkish, that foundational assumption shatters. The root cause is a profound mismatch between English-centric programming logic and the unique dual-form nature of the Turkish alphabet, where the letter "i" splits into dotted (İ/i) and dotless (I/ı) variants. To understand why enterprise software, databases, and video games suddenly crash to a black screen, you must look at what happens inside memory when a standard casing method like ToUpper() is executed. entry.title: A two-minute pre-stream routine for an avatar camera
entry.summary: Going live feels less rushed when the final checks have a fixed order. Use a two-minute timer as a stopping rule, not as a reason to ignore a problem. If a check fails, postpone the stream and fix it off-air. First 30 seconds: check the destination. Confirm the intended channel and stream privacy setting. Keep the broadcast stopped. Read the current scene name aloud so you do not accidentally start on a holding screen or a scene from yesterday. Next 30 seconds: check sound. Speak at your normal level, then pause. Watch the microphone meter during both parts. Unexpected movement during silence can reveal a second microphone, desktop playback, or a noisy input. Avoid monitoring through speakers that can feed back. Next 30 seconds: check the avatar. Make a short sentence and a gentle turn. Confirm the character, crop, and background in the final output, not just the source window. LiveSwap is one browser-based avatar camera you can use in this step. Final 30 seconds: prepare a pause. Locate your mute control and holding scene. Keep a simple note with the opening topic beside the monitor. Then start deliberately, rather than clicking through a chain of dialogs while already live.

entry.title: Why Web Apps Need Engineering, Not Just "Vibe Coding
entry.summary: Coding" The Hidden Traps of Vibe Coding Bullet Looks Good, Breaks Easily: AI checks if the screen looks right, not if the app handles real-world stress or errors. Bullet The "Black Box" Problem: If you don’t understand the code AI wrote, you won't know how to fix it when it crashes. Bullet Instant Mess: AI often writes messy, repetitive code that gets harder to work with every time you add a new feature. What Goes Wrong in Real Life Bullet Security Holes: AI-generated apps often leave doors open for hackers—like exposed passwords, missing login checks, or unprotected data. Bullet Broken Data: When multiple users click around at the same time, poorly structured databases can lose or corrupt important information. Bullet Impossible to Update: Without a clean layout, changing one small button or page later can accidentally break the rest of the website. How to Use AI the Right Way You don't have to stop using AI—just treat yourself as the architect and AI as your assistant: Plan your data first: Decide how your database is organized before asking AI to write code. Keep things separate: Keep your design, logic, and database code in separate, organized files. Check every line: Never blindly copy-paste. Review AI code carefully for security and edge cases. Use automated checks: Rely on testing tools to catch hidden bugs before your users do. Prompts can build a fast demo, but solid software engineering is what builds a reliable product.

entry.title: Test an avatar camera in OBS preview without going live
entry.summary: An OBS preview is a useful rehearsal space for an avatar feed, but it is not proof that a meeting participant sees the same output. Treat rehearsal and delivery as separate tests. Start with a new scene containing only the intended avatar source. Keep streaming and recording stopped while you arrange it. Fit the source to the canvas, then inspect whether the aspect ratio stretches the face or crops normal movement. A source that looks tidy in its own browser window can be misframed inside a different canvas. Record a short local clip with speech, a slow head turn, and a few seconds of stillness. Replay the file rather than relying on the moving preview. Listen for accidental duplicate microphone capture and watch for overlays that should not reach a work call. If you plan to send OBS Virtual Camera into a meeting app, start that output and select it in a private test meeting. Confirm the scene with a colleague before joining a larger call. The receiving app may crop or mirror its self-view differently. LiveSwap is a browser-based avatar camera that can be part of this workflow. Keep a clean rehearsal scene so you can evaluate the output without broadcasting your experiments.
